Calibration
HART Communicator Calibration: Sensor Trim, Output Trim, Rerange and Loop Test of a Pressure Transmitter With a Solved Example and mA Error Calculator

A HART communicator lets you talk to a smart transmitter, but it cannot calibrate anything without a known pressure source and an accurate meter. This guide shows the full bench and field routine, the trims, the common mistakes and a quick mA error calculator.

Sensor Trim Analog Output Trim Rerange vs Calibration 250 Ω Loop Resistor mA Error Calculator

Learn how to calibrate a HART pressure transmitter with an Emerson 475, AMS Trex or Fluke 754, from the as found test to the as left record. Includes the trim sequence, a common errors table and an mA error calculator.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn hart communicator calibration of a smart pressure transmitter, step by step, with sensor trim, output trim and a solved example.
Quick Answer

How to do HART communicator calibration on a smart pressure transmitter?

HART communicator calibration means checking a smart transmitter against a reference pressure and a precision mA meter, then trimming it until both agree. The key check is expected current = 4 + 16 × (pressure ÷ span). For example, 5 bar on a 0 to 10 bar range must give 12.000 mA, and a reading of 12.05 mA is 0.31 % of span high.

  1. Connect the handheld across at least 250 Ω of loop resistance
  2. Record as found readings at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 %
  3. Apply reference pressure and do the lower and upper sensor trim
  4. Do analog output trim at 4 and 20 mA with a precision meter
  5. Repeat the five point test and save the as left record

What Is HART Communicator Calibration?

HART communicator calibration is the process of testing a smart transmitter against a known reference and then using a HART handheld to trim its sensor reading and its 4 to 20 mA output so both match the standard. The communicator only sends digital commands, while a pressure calibrator and a precision milliammeter provide the real proof of accuracy.

Key Facts
  • Connect the handheld across a loop with at least 250 Ω of resistance
  • Record an as found test at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 % of range
  • Do sensor trim (lower and upper) with a reference pressure applied
  • Do analog output trim at 4 and 20 mA with a precision meter
  • Repeat the five point test and save the as left record

A smart transmitter has two converters inside, an analog to digital stage that reads the sensor and a digital to analog stage that drives the loop current. Our guide on sensor trim and output trim explains these blocks in depth, and this article shows how to use them with a handheld in the field.

Advertisement

Tools You Need for HART Communicator Calibration

Fluke notes that a communicator on its own can read and change configuration but cannot measure or source an analog value. That is why every hart communicator calibration needs a reference such as a dead weight pressure tester or a multifunction process calibrator alongside the handheld.

Emerson 475 Field Communicator

Classic handheld with HART and Fieldbus support and a large device description library.

Best for: Configuration, trims, rerange in the field
Legacy
Emerson AMS Trex

Newer touch screen communicator that Emerson says can also power a HART device on the bench.

Best for: Field and workshop trims
Current
Fluke 754 Documenting Calibrator

Measures mA, sources and reads pressure with modules and talks HART in one box.

Best for: As found and as left records
All in One
Pressure Source and Reference

Hand pump with a reference gauge, pressure module or dead weight tester.

Best for: Applying known inputs
Essential
Do You Know?

Fluke states that industry practice expects the measurement standard to be 4 to 10 times more accurate than the device under test. A 0.075 % transmitter therefore needs a pressure module, not a dial gauge.

How to Connect a HART Communicator With a 250 Ω Resistor

HART needs a minimum loop resistance of about 250 Ω so the digital current signal develops a readable voltage. Our article on the HART loop resistor shows why the handheld fails to find the device when this resistor is missing.

Loop Supply24 V DC from the DCS card or a bench supply
250 Ω ResistorIn series, gives the HART signal a voltage to read
TransmitterTwo wire smart device under test
Precision mA MeterIn series to read the true loop current
Communicator LeadsAcross the resistor or across the transmitter terminals

The resistor also eats supply voltage, because 20 mA through 250 Ω drops 5 V before the transmitter gets anything. A quick refresher on Ohm law and Kirchhoff voltage law helps you check that the transmitter still has its minimum lift off voltage at full scale.

Quick Tip

On a bench with a 24 V supply, a 250 Ω resistor and a long cable, check the voltage at the transmitter terminals at 20 mA before you start. Use our HART loop voltage budget calculator if the margin looks tight.

Rerange vs Calibration: Is Rerange the Same as Calibration?

No, rerange only changes the LRV and URV numbers that define which pressures map to 4 and 20 mA, and it does not correct any sensor error. Calibration compares the transmitter against a reference and, if needed, trims the sensor or the output so readings match the standard.

Rerange (Configuration)
  • Changes LRV and URV in memory
  • Needs no reference pressure when keyed in
  • Like zero and span on an analog transmitter
  • Does not fix sensor drift
Calibration (Trim and Verify)
  • Compares output with a traceable standard
  • Needs a known pressure and an accurate meter
  • Sensor trim corrects the digital PV
  • Output trim corrects the mA signal

Fluke explains that for a loop using only the 4 to 20 mA signal, rerange, analog output trim and zero trim are the relevant adjustments. If the host also reads the digital PV over HART, a sensor trim becomes necessary, which is also why the process variables in HART transmitters must be checked one by one.

Myth: Changing LRV and URV from the handheld calibrates the transmitter.
Fact: That is only a rerange, and the sensor error stays exactly where it was.
Myth: A zero trim is the same as a full sensor trim.
Fact: Zero trim is a single point offset fix, while a full sensor trim corrects both the lower and upper sensor points.
Myth: If the handheld shows the right PV, the loop is fine.
Fact: The digital PV can be correct while the mA output is off, so always read the real current with a meter.

HART Communicator Calibration Step by Step for a Pressure Transmitter

The sequence below follows the order used by Fluke and by Emerson in its Rosemount 3051 manual: test first, trim the sensor, trim the output, then verify. Doing hart communicator calibration in this order stops one correction from hiding another.

1
Permit and Isolate
Get the permit, inform the panel operator and put the loop in manual or bypass.
2
Isolate the Process
Close the manifold block valves, vent the transmitter and connect the test hose.
3
Connect the Loop
Wire the supply, 250 Ω resistor, precision meter and communicator as shown above.
4
Read the Configuration
Note tag, LRV, URV, units, damping, transfer function and alarm direction.
5
As Found Test
Apply 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 % pressure rising, then falling, and record PV and mA.
6
Sensor Trim
With reference pressure applied, run lower sensor trim then upper sensor trim.
7
Analog Output Trim
Command 4 mA, enter the meter reading, then repeat at 20 mA.
8
As Left Test
Repeat the five point test and confirm every point is within tolerance.
9
Restore and Record
Reconnect the process, return the loop to the operator and save the certificate.

Record the as found readings before you touch anything, because they show how much the instrument drifted since the last visit. The format for those sheets is covered in our article on the calibration certificate with as found and as left data.

Do You Know?

Emerson describes the analog output trim as a digital to analog trim, and its manuals ask for a precision ammeter in the loop.

Sensor Trim vs Output Trim: What Is the Difference?

Think of the sensor trim as fixing what the transmitter believes, and the output trim as fixing what it tells the DCS. A transmitter can need one, both or neither, which you only learn from a careful hart communicator calibration as found test.

PointSensor TrimAnalog Output Trim
Converter adjustedAnalog to digital (input)Digital to analog (output)
Reference neededKnown pressure sourcePrecision mA meter
CorrectsDigital PV reading4 and 20 mA loop current
Typical pointsLower and upper, or zero only4 mA then 20 mA
When to useDigital PV used or sensor drift foundmA output off with correct PV

Solved Example and mA Error Calculator

A 0 to 10 bar transmitter receives 5 bar from the reference, and the precision meter reads 12.05 mA. The tolerance is 0.5 % of span, so this hart communicator calibration point must stay inside that limit.

Range 0 to 10 bar, span 16 mA
Expected = 4 + 16 × (5 ÷ 10)
Expected = 12.000 mA
Error = (12.05 minus 12.000) ÷ 16 × 100
Error = 0.31 % of span, PASS
HART Transmitter mA Error Calculator
Result at this test point
Expected 12.000 mA, error 0.31 % of span, PASS at 0.5 % tolerance

Use the same calculator for every point of the five point test and write the error next to each reading. You can also check the result with the online calibration error tool or our calibration error calculation guide.

If errors grow steadily from 0 % to 100 %, the cause is usually span, while a constant error at every point points to zero. Our article on offset, zero and span error shows how to read these patterns quickly.

Advertisement

Loop Test With a HART Communicator

The loop test command forces the transmitter to output a fixed current, such as 4, 12 or 20 mA, without any pressure applied. Used at the end of hart communicator calibration, it proves the wiring, the DCS input card scaling and the alarms, as described in our pressure transmitter loop check procedure.

Fault currents below 3.6 mA and above 21 mA come from the NAMUR NE 43 recommendation, explained in our page on NAMUR NE 43. Always end the loop test from the handheld, or the transmitter may stay fixed at the forced current.

Common Errors in HART Communicator Calibration

Most failed calibrations come from a missing loop resistor, a poor reference, leaking test hoses or trimming in the wrong order. The table below lists each symptom with its likely cause and fix.

SymptomLikely CauseField Fix
No device foundLoop resistance below 250 ΩAdd resistor or connect across it
PV correct, mA wrongOutput stage driftRun analog output trim
mA wrong at all points equallyZero offset or mounting effectZero trim with ports vented
Error grows toward 20 mASpan errorFull lower and upper sensor trim
Reading jumps or settles slowlyHigh damping or leakCheck damping value and test hose
Trim rejected by deviceTrim points too close or wrong unitsUse LRV and URV points in correct units
Quick Tip

Never trim a transmitter against the same meter you used to find the error unless that meter is traceable and better than the device. Our page on the calibration traceability chain explains why the reference must carry a valid certificate.

  • Permit taken for hart communicator calibration and loop placed in manual
  • Reference pressure standard within its calibration date
  • At least 250 Ω in the loop for HART
  • As found test recorded at five points
  • Sensor trim done at LRV and URV points
  • Output trim done at 4 and 20 mA
  • As left test within tolerance and certificate saved

When a transmitter fails the as left test of a hart communicator calibration even after a full trim, move to fault finding instead of repeating trims. Our pressure transmitter troubleshooting guide covers impulse lines, diaphragm damage and electronics faults.

HART Communicator Calibration FAQ

Can you calibrate a pressure transmitter using only a HART communicator?

No, a handheld alone cannot calibrate a transmitter because it has no reference pressure and no accurate current meter. It can only rerange the device and run trim commands.

You also need a pressure reference about 4 times more accurate than the device and a precision milliammeter.

What is the difference between sensor trim and output trim in HART transmitters?

Sensor trim corrects the analog to digital stage so the digital pressure value matches a reference pressure. Output trim corrects the 4 to 20 mA loop current against a precision meter.

Do the sensor trim first, because the output depends on the digital value.

How to calculate the mA error of a HART transmitter step by step?

Find the expected current as 4 plus 16 times the applied pressure divided by span. Subtract it from the measured current, divide by 16 mA and multiply by 100.

For example, 5 bar on a 0 to 10 bar range expects 12.000 mA, so 12.05 mA is 0.31 % high.

Why is a 250 ohm resistor needed for HART communication on the bench?

About 250 ohms turns the small HART current changes into a readable voltage, and without it the handheld usually finds no device.

The resistor drops 5 volts at 20 mA, so a 24 volt supply leaves about 19 volts for the transmitter and cable.

What is the most common mistake in hart communicator calibration of transmitters?

The most common mistake is doing a rerange and calling it calibration, because rerange never compares the device with a standard. Another is trimming against an uncertified meter.

Always record as found readings first, use traceable references and repeat the five point test after every trim.

How often should a HART pressure transmitter be calibrated in a process plant?

Many plants start with a 12 month interval and adjust it using as found history. Safety loops follow the proof test interval in the safety requirements specification.

If errors stay well within tolerance for three cycles, the interval can often grow to 24 months.

What We Learn Today

  • HART communicator calibration needs a known pressure source and a precision meter, because the handheld alone can only configure and trim the transmitter.
  • Sensor trim corrects the analog to digital stage while analog output trim corrects the 4 and 20 mA current that the DCS actually receives.
  • Rerange changes only the LRV and URV values, so always record as found and as left readings at five points to prove real accuracy.
